title: json vs jsonb; the operators ->, ->>, @>, ?
summary: -> walks a jsonb document and keeps jsonb, ->> ends the walk with text; a JSON null and a missing key are different things. @> tests whether a document contains a shape, ? whether a key or string element exists. ||, -, #-, jsonb_set and subscripts change documents, with traps around NULL.

examples.title: Navigating a document: ->, ->>, #>>, array indexes, and JSON null vs SQL NULL

annotations.note: -> returns jsonb: number_jsonb is the JSON number 108, still of type jsonb. ->> returns text: main, without the quotes. Walk with -> and use ->> only at the last step, when you want the value.
#>> takes the whole path as a text array. Event 2 has no agent, and the docs' rule applies: extraction operators return NULL instead of failing when the document doesn't have the requested structure.
JSON array positions are 0-based, unlike SQL arrays (1-based), and -1 is the last element. Event 2's empty tags array has no element 0, which is NULL again rather than an error.

Event 1 has "retry_of": null, event 2 has no such key. -> returns the JSON value null for the first (a real jsonb value, so IS NULL is false) and SQL NULL for the second. ->> turns both into SQL NULL. Only ? and jsonb_typeof tell them apart.
'9' > '100' as text, because the character 9 sorts after 1, so event 2 passes a filter it should fail. The same happens in ORDER BY on a ->> value.
Two correct forms: cast the text (an expression index can serve this one, see the indexing lesson), or compare jsonb with jsonb, which compares numbers numerically.
SQLSTATE 42883: there is no text = integer operator. Compare with a string ('108'), cast, or ask with containment: payload @> '{"build": {"number": 108}}'.

examples.title: @> containment and the ? existence operators, and what json lacks

annotations.note: Containment is anchored at the root: the pattern's shape must match the document's from the top. {"branch": "main"} would need a top-level branch key, and no event has one.
Array containment ignores order and duplicates: ["smoke", "nightly"] is contained in ["nightly", "smoke"]. Event 2 has only smoke.

A string is not a one-element array: {"tags": "smoke"} matches nothing. The docs' exception, an array containing a bare primitive, shows up when you compare the array itself, as payload -> 'tags' @> '"smoke"' does.

A pattern element matches any array element that contains it: some result has status failed. A pattern object with two keys must find both in the same element; status from one result and test from another don't combine.
? looks at top-level keys only. branch lives under build, so nested_key is false everywhere; payload -> 'build' ? 'branch' would be true.
On an array, ? tests for string elements; ?| means any of the list, ?& all of it. Strings only: '[1, 2]'::jsonb ? '1' is false.
jsonb compares numbers as numbers and objects key by key, so the two documents are equal. It still prints 120.0 as written: JSON numbers are stored as numeric, which keeps trailing zeros.
SQLSTATE 42883. json stores the text and offers only the extraction operators (->, ->>, #>, #>>): no containment, existence, equality or GIN index. Cast to jsonb, or store jsonb in the first place.

examples.title: Changing documents: shallow ||, subscripts, jsonb_set, - and #-, and the NULL trap

annotations.note: || merges top-level keys, and the right side's value wins whole: notify lost email. The docs say it outright: || does not operate recursively.
Subscript assignment (PG 14) creates or replaces one nested value. The right-hand side must be jsonb, hence the quoted 'true'.
jsonb_set does the same with a text[] path, and adds the key because create_if_missing defaults to true. All earlier steps of the path must exist, or the document comes back unchanged.
- removes a top-level key, #- removes the value at a path. Both are ordinary operators, applied left to right here.

to_jsonb(NULL) is SQL NULL, and jsonb_set returns NULL when given one. In an UPDATE that sets the whole column to NULL, or fails if it is NOT NULL. jsonb_set_lax (PG 13) writes a JSON null by default, or deletes the key, raises an error or returns the document unchanged.

use_cases: Reading fields from stored webhook payloads, third-party API responses and event logs
Filtering semi-structured rows by shape: events on branch main with any failed result (@>)
Per-project settings and feature flags: test for a key (?), change one nested value (subscripts, jsonb_set)
String lists inside documents, such as tags: ?| for any of, ?& for all of
strengths: @> says 'has this nested shape' in one operator that a GIN index can serve, where Go or Java code would decode and walk the tree
Extraction never throws on a missing key or a different shape; it returns NULL, which suits documents whose structure varies
jsonb comparisons are semantic: key order, whitespace and 120 vs 120.0 don't matter, unlike comparing JSON text
Partial updates (subscripts, jsonb_set, -, #-) happen inside one UPDATE, without a read-modify-write round trip through the application
weaknesses: ->> returns text, so numbers and dates need casts, and a forgotten cast compares strings without any error
A missing key, a JSON null and a mistyped path all come back as NULL through ->>, so a typo in a key name fails silently
|| is shallow and jsonb_set returns NULL for a NULL value: two easy ways to lose data in an UPDATE
Changing one key writes a new version of the whole row and locks it, so big, frequently updated documents contend

pitfalls.title: Comparing ->> output as text
pitfalls.detail: '9' > '100' is true for strings. Cast the extracted text, or compare jsonb values.

pitfalls.title: Testing a JSON null with -> ... IS NULL
pitfalls.detail: -> returns the JSON value null, which is not SQL NULL. If null and missing mean the same to you, test the ->> result; if they differ, use ? or jsonb_typeof.

pitfalls.title: Deep merge with ||
pitfalls.detail: The right-hand object replaces the left one's nested objects whole. Set the nested value instead.
pitfalls.bad: UPDATE project_settings SET prefs = prefs || '{"notify": {"slack": true}}'

pitfalls.title: jsonb_set with a value that may be NULL
pitfalls.detail: A NULL parameter makes jsonb_set return NULL, and the UPDATE erases the document (or fails on NOT NULL). Use jsonb_set_lax and say what NULL should mean.

pitfalls.title: Casting a JSON null on older servers
pitfalls.detail: Since PostgreSQL 18, (payload -> 'retry_of')::int returns NULL for a JSON null; earlier versions raise an error. Code that must also run on older servers should cast the ->> text instead.

quiz.q: payload is {"retry_of": null}. What does `payload -> 'retry_of' IS NULL` return?
quiz.why: -> returns the JSON value null, a non-NULL jsonb value. ->> would return SQL NULL.

options: true, because b is in the array
false, because inside an object a string doesn't match an array
quiz.why: Containment compares structure from the root; the primitive-in-array exception only applies when the array itself is compared, as in payload -> 'tags' @> '"b"'.

quiz.q: build.number is 9 in one row and 108 in another. Which condition selects only 108?
quiz.why: The first compares text ('9' > '100' is true); the third looks for a top-level number key, which doesn't exist.

quiz.q: prefs is {"notify": {"email": true, "slack": false}}. What is `prefs || '{"notify": {"slack": true}}'`?
quiz.why: || merges only the top level; the right side's notify object replaces the left one whole.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: json and jsonb operators
PostgreSQL docs: jsonb Containment and Existence
PostgreSQL docs: JSON processing functions (jsonb_set, jsonb_set_lax)

body:
## Concept

The jsonb lesson in the types module showed the storage difference: `json` keeps an exact copy of the
input text, `jsonb` stores it parsed (keys deduplicated and reordered, whitespace gone).
For querying, the consequence is that `json` only has the four extraction operators;
everything else in this lesson is `jsonb`-only. Use `json` when the exact text matters,
for example a webhook body whose signature was computed over its bytes, and `jsonb` for
everything you query.

The operators, by job:

- **Navigate:** `->` takes a key or a 0-based array index (negative counts from the
  end) and returns `jsonb`; `->>` does the same and returns `text`; `#>` and `#>>` take a
  whole path as `text[]`. A path that doesn't exist yields NULL, never an error.
- **Null:** a key holding JSON `null` is not the same as a missing key. `->` returns
  the jsonb value `null` for the first and SQL NULL for the second; `->>` returns SQL
  NULL for both.
- **Test:** `@>` asks whether the left document contains the right one's shape (`<@`
  is the reverse). `?`, `?|` and `?&` ask whether a string exists as a top-level key or
  as a string element of an array.
- **Change:** `||` merges or concatenates (shallowly), `-` and `#-` delete, `jsonb_set`
  and subscript assignment (`doc['a']['b'] = ...`, PG 14) replace one nested value.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS:** `payload #>> '{build,agent,os}'` is `payload?.build?.agent?.os`, with NULL for
  `undefined`. JSON null versus a missing key is JS's `null` versus `undefined`, and
  `payload ? 'retry_of'` is `'retry_of' in payload`.
- **Python:** `->` chains are `d.get('build', {}).get('agent')`; `?` is `key in d`;
  `@>` is a recursive "is a subset of" check that you would otherwise write by hand.
- **Go:** decoding into a struct, a `*int` field is nil both for `null` and for a
  missing key, so Go can't tell them apart without `json.RawMessage` or a map lookup;
  SQL can, with `?`. pgx uses `$1` placeholders, so the `?` operators cause no trouble.
- **Java:** JDBC uses `?` as the parameter placeholder. With PgJDBC, write the operators
  as `??` in a `PreparedStatement`, or use `@>`, which has no question mark.
- **Everyone:** `->>` hands you text. Comparisons and sorting on it are text operations
  until you cast, whereas a JSON decoder in your language would have given you 108 as a
  number.

## Design notes

Filter with operators an index can serve and extract in the `SELECT` list. `WHERE
payload @> '{"build": {"branch": "main"}}'` and `WHERE payload -> 'build' ->> 'branch' =
'main'` ask the same question, but only the first can use a GIN index on `payload` (the
GIN lesson); the second needs an expression index of its own (the indexing lesson in this
module).

Decide once what "absent" means. If a JSON `null` and a missing key mean the same thing,
strip nulls on write (`jsonb_strip_nulls`) or always test the `->>` result; if they
differ, test with `?` and say so in a comment.

Update narrowly: subscripts or `jsonb_set` for nested values, `jsonb_set_lax` when the
new value comes from a parameter that may be NULL, and `||` only for top-level keys.
Every one of these writes a new version of the whole row and takes its row lock. A key
that several writers update independently, or that every query filters on, has outgrown
the document; the indexing lesson shows how to promote it to a column.

PostgreSQL 18 changed one detail: casting a JSON `null` to a scalar type, as in
`(payload -> 'retry_of')::int`, now returns NULL; earlier versions raise an error.

files.examples/01_navigate.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.json.jsonb-operators): -> keeps jsonb, ->> gives text; JSON null is not SQL NULL.
CREATE TABLE ci_events (
  id      int   PRIMARY KEY,
  payload jsonb NOT NULL          -- a CI webhook body, stored as received
);
INSERT INTO ci_events VALUES
  (1, '{"build": {"number": 108, "branch": "main", "agent": {"os": "linux"}},
        "results": [{"test": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 120},
                    {"test": "Çıkış", "status": "failed", "ms": 85}],
        "tags": ["nightly", "smoke"], "retry_of": null}'),
  (2, '{"build": {"number": 9, "branch": "feature/kvkk"},
        "results": [{"test": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 130}],
        "tags": []}');

-- Chain -> to walk down, or give #> / #>> the whole path. JSON arrays
-- are 0-based, and negative indexes count from the end.
SELECT id,
       payload -> 'build' -> 'number'          AS number_jsonb,
       payload -> 'build' ->> 'branch'         AS branch_text,
       payload #>> '{build,agent,os}'          AS agent_os,
       payload -> 'results' -> 0 ->> 'test'    AS first_test,
       payload -> 'results' -> -1 ->> 'status' AS last_status,
       payload -> 'tags' ->> 0                 AS first_tag
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- A key holding JSON null and a missing key look alike through ->>.
SELECT id,
       payload -> 'retry_of'               AS arrow,
       payload -> 'retry_of' IS NULL       AS arrow_is_null,
       payload ->> 'retry_of' IS NULL      AS text_is_null,
       payload ? 'retry_of'                AS has_key,
       jsonb_typeof(payload -> 'retry_of') AS json_type
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- ->> returns text, and text compares character by character.
SELECT id,
       payload -> 'build' ->> 'number' > '100'      AS as_text,
       (payload -> 'build' ->> 'number')::int > 100 AS as_int,
       payload -> 'build' -> 'number' > '100'       AS as_jsonb
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- Text on the left, a number on the right: no operator matches.
SELECT id FROM ci_events WHERE payload -> 'build' ->> 'number' = 108;
files.examples/02_containment.sql:
CREATE TABLE ci_events (
  id      int   PRIMARY KEY,
  payload jsonb NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO ci_events VALUES
  (1, '{"build": {"branch": "main"}, "tags": ["nightly", "smoke"],
        "results": [{"test": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 120},
                    {"test": "Çıkış", "status": "failed", "ms": 85}]}'),
  (2, '{"build": {"branch": "feature/kvkk"}, "tags": ["smoke"],
        "results": [{"test": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 130}]}'),
  (3, '{"build": {"branch": "main"}, "tags": [], "results": [], "retry_of": 1}');

-- @> asks: does the left document contain this shape? Nested objects match
-- at the same path; array elements match in any order; extra keys are ignored.
SELECT id,
       payload @> '{"build": {"branch": "main"}}'         AS on_main,
       payload @> '{"branch": "main"}'                     AS wrong_level,
       payload @> '{"tags": ["smoke", "nightly"]}'         AS both_tags,
       payload @> '{"tags": "smoke"}'                      AS scalar_tag,
       payload -> 'tags' @> '"smoke"'                      AS array_has_smoke,
       payload @> '{"results": [{"status": "failed"}]}'    AS any_failed
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- ? and friends test strings: top-level keys, or string elements of an array.
SELECT id,
       payload ? 'retry_of'                          AS has_retry,
       payload ? 'branch'                            AS nested_key,
       payload -> 'tags' ? 'smoke'                   AS smoke,
       payload -> 'tags' ?| ARRAY['nightly', 'perf'] AS any_of,
       payload -> 'tags' ?& ARRAY['nightly', 'smoke'] AS all_of
FROM ci_events
ORDER BY id;

-- jsonb equality is structural and numeric: 120.0 = 120, key order is irrelevant.
SELECT '{"ms": 120.0, "test": "Giriş"}'::jsonb
         = '{"test": "Giriş", "ms": 120}'::jsonb AS equal,
       '{"ms": 120.0}'::jsonb                    AS kept_as_written;

-- The plain json type stores text and has none of these operators.
SELECT payload::json @> '{"tags": ["smoke"]}' FROM ci_events;
